restrictions.summary: Ordinary citizens have no open access to the global internet. Unauthorised circumvention tools, including VPNs, are illegal and can carry extreme penalties under the regime's information-control laws.

The state-monopoly ISP blocks the vast majority of foreign services and actively suppresses VPNs and other circumvention tools. Applicants for home internet have been required to pledge not to use bypass tools; unauthorised use can bring multi-year sentences.

Belarusian law restricts anonymisers and VPN services used to access blocked resources. Authorities have blocked major commercial VPN providers and pursued users and operators of circumvention tools, especially around protests.
Iraq imposed a blanket ban on VPN use during the fight against ISIS; the prohibition has largely remained in force with periodic enforcement against providers and users of unauthorised tunnels.

Unlicensed commercial VPNs for public cross-border access are illegal. Only government-approved / licensed international channels (typically enterprise) are permitted; unauthorised consumer VPNs face blocking, provider crackdowns, and occasional user penalties.

VPNs that refuse to cooperate with Roskomnadzor’s blocked-sites registry face nationwide blocking; the 2025–2026 crackdown has blocked hundreds of VPN services and popular protocols, banned VPN advertising, and pressed operators and platforms to detect and throttle VPN traffic. A law passed in July 2025 (in force that September) also fines intentional searches for 'extremist' material — explicitly including via VPN — raising liability for ordinary circumvention.

Iran criminalised use of non-approved VPNs (2024), pairing the ban with deep-packet inspection that disrupts common protocols—especially during protests. Only government-sanctioned tunnels are considered lawful.

restrictions.since: Functional ban from May 2024; Cybersecurity Law in force 1 Jan 2025
restrictions.summary: What began as a functional VPN blackout in May 2024 was codified into law on 1 January 2025: the junta's Cybersecurity Law makes unauthorised VPN installation or use a criminal offence, punishable by up to six months in prison and fines of roughly $480–4,750, with no lawful route for ordinary citizens to obtain an approved VPN. Soldiers and police conduct random phone searches for VPN apps and make arrests on the spot, and the law's extraterritorial clause even threatens Myanmar nationals living abroad.

Owning a VPN is not a blanket crime, but using one to access blocked services (e.g. unlicensed VoIP, gambling, other restricted content) is a serious offence under UAE cybercrime rules, with very large fines reported for misuse.
Unauthorised use of encryption tools without TRA permission is prohibited. Enforcement focuses on misuse to reach blocked services; TRA has publicly warned against unapproved VPN products.

restrictions.since: CERT-In Direction No. V — in force 28 June 2022
restrictions.summary: VPNs stay legal to use, but a 2022 CERT-In cybersecurity directive orders providers running servers in India to log extensive customer data — validated subscriber names, hire dates, IP addresses allotted and used, emails, physical addresses and contact numbers — and retain it for at least five years, even after an account is closed. Rather than comply with the logging mandate, major providers such as ExpressVPN, NordVPN and Surfshark pulled their physical servers out of the country and now route Indian IPs through virtual servers hosted abroad.

restrictions.since: PTA registration drive from 2024; CVAS-Data licensing from Nov 2025
restrictions.summary: Pakistan is corralling VPNs into a state licensing regime rather than banning them outright. From late 2024 the PTA pressed users and firms to register VPNs and began blocking 'unregistered' or 'illegal' services — after the Council of Islamic Ideology branded unregulated VPNs un-Islamic — and in November 2025 it started issuing Class VAS (CVAS-Data) licences to approved local providers. Only licensed, PTA-overseen VPNs are sanctioned, while unlicensed apps face intermittent blocking and disruption.

legislative_efforts.title: Age-verification rollout and VPN-circumvention debate
legislative_efforts.status: Policy discussion — no EU-wide VPN ban enacted
legislative_efforts.summary: As member states and the Commission push privacy-preserving age checks for social platforms, some officials have floated measures against tools that bypass age gates (including VPNs). No pan-EU criminal ban is in force; proposals remain contested.

rejected_efforts.title: SB 130 and related state efforts targeting VPN use for restricted content
rejected_efforts.status: Rejected — advanced in legislature then failed amid civil-liberties backlash
rejected_efforts.summary: Wisconsin saw a high-profile 2025 attempt (SB 130) that would have constrained VPN use in connection with age-restricted material—an early serious state-level VPN restriction effort that did not become law after political pushback.

countries.name: China
countries.note: All VPN apps removed from the China App Store since July 2017; Google Play does not operate in mainland China; provider sites blocked by the Great Firewall.

countries.name: Russia
countries.note: Apple has removed 100+ VPN apps from the Russian App Store since July 2024 and Roskomnadzor blocks roughly 200 VPN services; only individually verified cases are marked removed/blocked here, the rest show as no data or partial.

countries.name: Iran
countries.note: Apple operates no Iranian storefront (US sanctions; store access IP-blocked since 2018). Free VPN apps remain on Google Play but deep-packet inspection disrupts use; provider sites are filtered.

countries.name: Myanmar
countries.note: Apps are not delisted, but VPN downloads and traffic have been blocked at network level since 30 May 2024 and possession risks arrest; provider sites blocked.

countries.name: Turkmenistan
countries.note: The state-monopoly ISP filters circumvention tools and blocks most foreign VPN sites; store access is unreliable and uncertified encryption is banned.

countries.name: Belarus
countries.note: No store delistings reported; major VPN providers blocked at network level per May 2024 reports, with no public per-provider list.

countries.name: Pakistan
countries.note: Apps remain in stores; unregistered VPN services have been blocked under CVAS-Data licensing since 22 December 2025 — providers named in reporting are marked blocked.

countries.name: United Arab Emirates
countries.note: Apps remain in stores; some provider sites and protocols are disrupted via DPI and VPN misuse is criminalised.

countries.name: Oman
countries.note: Apps remain in stores; unapproved encryption is restricted and some provider sites are blocked.

countries.name: Iraq
countries.note: The 2014 blanket ban is largely unenforced today; no current per-provider documentation of store or website blocks.

countries.name: India
countries.note: No blocks — providers withdrew Indian servers over CERT-In logging rules, but apps and websites remain available.

countries.name: North Korea
countries.note: No public access to the global internet or foreign app stores.
